title: Down With Love
full_review:
The sassy author of a who-needs-men best seller falls hard for a chauvinistic, playboy journalist in the stylishly entertaining "Down With Love" (Fox).

Director Peyton Reed swipes a page from the '60s-era Doris Day-Rock Hudson romantic comedies in this Technicolor battle of the sexes. Yet while the film employs a groovy retro-lounge aesthetic of pillbox hats and velvet-toned Sinatra tunes, its thematic undercurrents are charged with contemporary, hot-button issues concerning sexual autonomy and gender politics.

"Down With Love" is set in the New York City of the halcyon 1960s -- the mythic Gotham of Hollywood, replete with paper moons, painted backdrops and rain that falls on cue. Into this fabled metropolis sashays Barbara Novak (Renee Zellweger), a small-town girl with an obligatory suitcase full of dreams whose book, the eponymous "Down With Love" -- a self-help, women's lib manifesto -- makes her an overnight celebrity.

Assigned by Know -- "the magazine for men in the know" -- to cover Novak's meteoric rise is Catch Block (Ewan McGregor), a lady-killing lounge lizard who lands Pulitzer Prizes as routinely as he does stewardesses. The "ladies-man, man's-man, man-about-town" ace journalist vows to expose Novak as a marriage-crazed fraud by charming her into falling in love with him, thus debunking her testosterone-wary tract.

To accomplish this, Catch goes undercover, posing as a demure Southern astronaut, Maj. Zip Martin. Despite her sworn-off-men policy, Novak's three-step program of female empowerment offers little resistance to Zip's aw-shucks advances. The rest of the film is a screwball bossa nova of deception as Catch begins to reel in his prey. Along the way they fall in love, throwing a wrench in Catch's ruse and making his conquest a Pyrrhic victory on more than one level.

"Down With Love" evokes a heightened glamour right from the jazzy opening credits. The New York presented is all artifice -- a romanticized set-piece crafted to reinforce the film's enchanted moonstruck milieu.

McGregor is on the money as the martini-toting cad -- the perfect blend of Rat Pack cool and James Bond savoir faire. And Zellweger, whose on-screen chemistry with McGregor clicks from the start, imbues Novak with a balance of resiliency and girlish vulnerability. David Hyde Pierce brings his patented brand of understated comedy to the role of Peter McMannus, Catch's confidence-challenged best friend and editor, who is lovesick for Novak's feisty editor, Vikki (Sarah Paulson).

Playing on audiences' fascination with early-'60s fashion and design, Reed employs devices like split screens and period music to create what appears on the surface to be an old-fashioned romantic comedy while reinventing the genre with gender reversals more in tune with "modern" sensibilities. True to its source -- Day-Hudson collaborations such as "Pillow Talk" -- the film eschews overt sexual situations, conveying the characters' carnal obsessions through whip-smart wordplay, double entendres and cleverly suggestive image juxtaposition.

However, while there's still much to be said about the misogynistic treatment of women common in a male-dominated society, the film endorses a fatuous philosophy of liberation, dressed up in modish catch phrases and vintage couture and passed off as harmless humor. Novak's book -- a pre-feminist do-it-yourself manual to sexual libertinism -- purports that love is a game you can master by adopting men's no-strings, sex-a-la-carte attitude, freeing women from the shackles of commitment and marriage and fostering equality in the workplace. And though much of the premise revolves around Catch trying to disprove such cynical claims, the message viewers are left with falls far short of love conquers all.

Though in love with Catch, Novak must sublimate her true feelings for the greater cause: the empowerment of women to indulge in the same sort of promiscuity that infuriates her about men. Rather than working to elevate both sexes to the pedestal of mutual dignity, Novak is content to offer her libidinous fans carte blanche to join men in the gutter.

Unfortunately, the love espoused by this film is not the meet-you-on-the-top-of-the-Empire-State-Building-with-tissues variety, but a watered-down hybrid with an attached prenuptial list of conditions. And while the happy ending seems to debunk assertions that the human heart is a game-board to be mastered by skill, it does allow for some "liberated" ground rules to be set -- as the McMannus and Vikki characters cooingly inform each other during the end-credit scrawl, "I love you, but I'm not giving up my career" -- a line of dialogue seven words too long.

Due to implied sexual situations, racy double entendres and sexually suggestive humor, as well as a misguided attitude toward sexual intimacy, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
